narrative:
The model predicts you have a 10% chance of failing your final year. While this is a low probability, it is high enough that the school requires you to take remedial courses as a precaution.

The prediction that you might fail is driven mainly by three aspects of your situation. The most influential factor is that you have had no past class failures. Surprisingly, this actually pushes the model toward expecting you might fail. Among students who passed, having zero previous failures is the average, yet in your specific combination of circumstances the model sees the complete lack of any prior academic struggle as a warning sign rather than a strength. 

The second strongest influence is your reason for choosing this school: you picked it for its reputation. This choice also pulls the prediction toward failing. Most students who ultimately passed chose the school for its specific courses instead.

Third, your weekly study time of 5–10 hours works in your favor and pulls the prediction back toward passing. However, this positive effect is not strong enough to outweigh the first two factors.

To improve, you should reflect on why having no past failures feels risky to the model in your case, consider whether your choice of school truly matches your needs, and think about increasing your study time beyond 5–10 hours each week. Taking the remedial courses seriously will give you extra support to turn this 10% risk into a clear pass. (218 words)
